verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a or 1b: the problem is stated, and 0001 fixes a latent bug at small cost. The one surviving objection, maintenance-fit-1, is a fixable design point at level 2 about 0002 having no loud failure when an allocation path does not record the page size. Only message #1 is visible and no code was read, so confidence is low.

brief.title: Fix pg_get_shmem_pagesize() on Windows and record page size in shmem header
brief.problem: pg_get_shmem_pagesize() returns zero on Windows when large pages are in use, because it calls GetHugePageSize(), which is a stub there. The only current caller, NUMA shared memory reporting, rejects Windows first, so no user sees the bug today. The author wants the function to be correct for future callers, including resizable shared memory.
brief.proposed_design: 0001 calls GetLargePageMinimum() on Windows when large pages are in use, and leaves the GetHugePageSize() stub and shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages unchanged. 0002 stores the page size in PGShmemHeader when the main segment is created, including the ordinary-page fallback with huge_pages=try. pg_get_shmem_pagesize() then returns the stored value, which 0002 sets again when shared memory is recreated.
user_visible_surface: C API: pg_get_shmem_pagesize() returns the large-page size on Windows instead of zero.
C API: PGShmemHeader in pg_shmem.h gains a field for the page size of the main segment.
author_claims: No current user-visible failure, so the fix targets master only with no backpatch.
0002 removes duplicated platform logic, so the accessor cannot disagree with the allocation code.
0002 avoids opening and scanning /proc/meminfo on every call on Linux, though the author measured no significant gain for the NUMA caller.
Resizable shared memory will need the page size during resizing and protection changes.
Earlier threads did not discuss the Windows stub returning zero or storing the page size in the header.
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible. Nobody has replied yet.
unclear: The proposal does not say whether PGShmemHeader layout changes affect extensions or tools that read the header.
The proposal does not say how sysv_shmem.c records the page size for each allocation method, such as mmap compared with System V.
The proposal does not say whether 0001 is still needed if 0002 is committed, other than for separate review.
The proposal does not say how 0002 was tested on Windows with large pages.

objections.title: Recorded page size has no check when an allocation path skips it
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch adds or changes an allocation path in sysv_shmem.c, for example for resizable shared memory, and does not set the new PGShmemHeader field. pg_get_shmem_pagesize() then returns zero or a stale value, and no test or build fails. Callers that compute alignment or page counts from it go wrong, and nobody notices until a user reports odd NUMA output or a resize failure.
objections.argument: Message #1 says 0002 relies on "every method of allocating shared memory will continue to record page size", so correctness moves from one accessor to each allocation path. sysv_shmem.c has several of these paths (huge-page mmap, ordinary mmap with the huge_pages=try fallback, System V), and win32_shmem.c has its own, so a future change has several places to miss. The proposal does not describe an assertion or other loud failure when the field is unset. shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages still uses GetHugePageSize(), so some duplicated page-size logic stays.
objections.author_must_show: What makes pg_get_shmem_pagesize() fail loudly, for example an assertion on a zero value, if a current or future allocation path does not record the page size?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 itself says 0002 depends on "hoping that every method of allocating shared memory will continue to record page size". The patch prose names no assertion or other loud failure for an unset field, so the request for one stands as a fixable point.

touch_points.reason: 0002 adds a field to PGShmemHeader in pg_shmem.h and changes what the exported pg_get_shmem_pagesize() returns on Windows.

touch_points.reason: Message #1 proposes master only, with no backpatch, because no current caller reaches the faulty path on Windows.

How does sysv_shmem.c record the page size for each allocation method: huge-page mmap, ordinary mmap after the huge_pages=try fallback, and System V?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the shared memory creation code in sysv_shmem.c and win32_shmem.c, including huge pages and Windows large pages. No committer has replied in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the rule that every allocation path records the page size in PGShmemHeader, for as long as the accessor reads it. Resizable shared memory would add callers that depend on it.
committability.author_follow_up: The author says he found this while working on resizable shared memory, which will use the function, so he has a reason to stay. The thread has no replies yet.

priority.reason: No user sees the bug today; the benefit goes to future callers on Windows and to resizable shared memory. The patches are small (1.8 KB and 6.4 KB), touch four files in the shared memory code, and add one header field.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody checked where the new field sits in PGShmemHeader, whether each allocation path sets it, or whether the Windows path behaves correctly with large pages.

precedents_retrieved.title: Supporting huge pages on Windows
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds huge_pages support on Windows by creating shared memory with SEC_LARGE_PAGES, which needs the "Lock pages in memory" user right. To keep that right in postgres, it changes pg_ctl so it no longer removes all privileges (DISABLE_MAX_PRIVILEGE) from the restricted token it uses to start the server.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to the pg_ctl change because it removes the containment that stripping all privileges gave the server process. They asked to keep that and add back only the needed privilege, but a token from CreateRestrictedToken() cannot gain privileges later, so the author's attempt failed. Magnus Hagander suggested listing the user's privileges with GetTokenInformation() and passing all but the needed ones to PrivilegesToDelete, and Andres Freund then proposed returning the patch with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Auto-tune shared_buffers to use available huge pages
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a setting (first huge_pages_autotune_buffers, later shared_buffers_autotune_target) that makes Postgres raise shared_buffers at startup until the shared memory request reaches a target size, such as the huge pages given to a Kubernetes pod. It moves the existing auto-tuning of other settings into dedicated functions so they use the configured shared_buffers, and adds a checkpoint_request_size GUC.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Ashutosh Bapat asked whether a script that finds the right shared_buffers with postgres -C is enough. The author replied that such a script must run before every start, which Docker images, Patroni and operators do not easily allow, and the thread had no further replies before the entry was withdrawn.

precedents_retrieved.title: Identify huge pages accessibility using madvise
precedents_retrieved.summary: With huge_pages = try, Postgres can map huge pages with MAP_HUGETLB inside a cgroup whose hugetlb limit is too low, and the first page fault then raises SIGBUS. The patch calls madvise with MADV_POPULATE_READ (Linux 5.14+) so that this case fails at startup and Postgres falls back to normal pages.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author found that since Linux 5.7 cgroups also limit hugetlb at reservation time (hugetlb.<size>.rsvd.limit_in_bytes), so a correct setup makes the mmap fail up front. Peter Eisentraut agreed that the kernel had addressed the issue and that the workaround was no longer needed. The entry was withdrawn, and users on older kernels or with orchestration tools that do not set the rsvd limit can apply the patch themselves.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Ah good, it looks like the issue was addressed properly in the kernel
then, and we don't need the workaround your patch proposes anymore.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support huge_pages on AIX
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets Postgres use large pages for System V shared memory on AIX, so huge_pages=try/on passes SHM_LGPAGE and SHM_PIN to shmget() when shared_memory_type = sysv. It was the second part of a set; the first part, the shared_memory_type GUC, was committed separately.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The AIX patch needed testing and adjustment on AIX, and the committer working on it, Thomas Munro, had no AIX access. He said he would withdraw it if it got no traction in that commitfest. The author was still testing in October 2019, and the visible messages do not show a result before the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It needs testing, review and (probably) adjustment from AIX users.

precedents_retrieved.title: Shared-memory based stats collector
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace the file-based stats collector with statistics kept in dynamic shared memory (dshash), so backends read stats without a stats file written by a separate process. The stats collector process goes away, and per-kind stats code moves into new files under utils/activity.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund reworked the patch in spring 2021 and judged it not committable for v14, citing weak test coverage, the need for architectural review and performance testing, an unresolved case where stats for dropped functions can be revived, and many open FIXMEs. A rebase then stalled on a new issue with partitioned tables. No new version was posted after July 2021, so the CommitFest manager marked the entry Returned with Feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Unfortunately I think
that, while it has gotten a lot closer, it's still about a week's worth of
work away from being committable.

precedents_retrieved.title: Optimize planner memory consumption for huge arrays
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch reduces planner memory use for large arrays in scalararraysel(), where each array element costs about 250 bytes and the cost multiplies with each partition. The first version freed the per-element Const and argument list after each selectivity call, and the discussion moved to a planner temporary memory context that is reset periodically.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane rejected the original per-call freeing as ad-hoc and posted a temporary-context patch instead. His measurements showed it barely reduced memory in the regression tests, and resetting after every use cost about 1% on pgbench -S. The thread ends on open design points: when to reset, a possible MemoryContextResetIfBig API, and turning the optimization off in debug builds. The visible messages do not show the final decision.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Even though this seems of only edge-case value, I'd much prefer to do this than the sort of ad-hoc patching initially proposed in this thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: NUMA shared memory interleaving
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a `numa` GUC that interleaves the shared memory segment, and later the parallel query DSM segments, across NUMA nodes with numa_interleave_memory(). Later versions add modes to restrict Postgres to a subset of nodes, for consolidation or isolation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra argued that blind interleaving ignores the internal structure of shared memory, so a buffer descriptor can land on a different node than its block, and all descriptors likely land on one node. He said later NUMA-aware work, such as per-node freelists, clocksweep and PGPROC placement, needs explicit per-structure placement and would have to largely undo this patch, and he questioned the node-subset configuration. Jakub Wartak agreed to wait for Tomas Vondra's own NUMA patch series, which was posted in a separate thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: But I just don't see how this could be 0001, followed by some later improvements. ISTM the improvements would have to largely undo 0001 first, and it would be nontrivial if an optimization needs to do that only for some part of the shared memory.

precedents_retrieved.title: WIP: Track relation size in shared memory
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pool of SMgrSharedRelation objects in shared memory that holds the authoritative size of each recently extended or truncated relation until the file is fsync'd, so backends stop calling lseek(SEEK_END). The aim was fewer system calls and correct sizes on filesystems such as NFS that can shrink files asynchronously; an earlier recovery-only size cache from the same thread was committed separately (c5315f4f).
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stayed at prototype stage. The author said a main piece was missing: a background process to clean dirty SR objects, so that foreground processes rarely block on fsync during eviction. Review comments from Buzhen, Andres and later Anastasia Lubennikova were still open, for example on CREATE DATABASE, which bypasses smgr, and on temporary relations. The visible messages show no reply after the July 2021 review before the entry was closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The main thing being: how can we clean these objects in the background?  That question being unanswered, there is a 0% chance of committing this in PostgreSQL 14.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. The earlier discussions cited in message #1 left shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages at -1 on Windows, and this proposal keeps that GUC and the GetHugePageSize() stub as they are, so the reason recorded there does not apply. Message #1 reports that no earlier thread discussed the stub returning zero or storing the page size in PGShmemHeader.

Neither patch touches SQL syntax, GUCs, pg_dump, psql, the wire protocol or on-disk data. The only contract change is a new field in PGShmemHeader, an in-memory structure that is rebuilt at each start, and the patches target master only, so the ABI rule for minor releases does not apply. shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages keeps its existing Windows behaviour, as earlier threads agreed. Without the code I could not check where the new field sits in PGShmemHeader or whether any extension reads the header layout directly.

The patches change only in-memory state: PGShmemHeader lives in the main shared memory segment and is rebuilt at each start and after crash reinitialization. Nothing reaches WAL, relation files, catalogs, pg_upgrade or the wire protocol. The header change is master-only, and extensions rarely read PGShmemHeader directly. Without the code, I could not check that the new field leaves the offsets of magic, creatorPID and the device/inode fields unchanged, which stale-segment detection reads.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It changes an internal C accessor and stores a page size in PGShmemHeader. The page size is already readable by any user through pg_shmem_allocations_numa and huge_page_size, and the patch adds no SQL-callable surface, role, or new data a non-superuser could reach.

Beyond the item above, the maintenance cost is small: a master-only bugfix with one header field, no hot-path cost, and no new external dependency. Need for 0002 rests on unmerged resizable shared memory, but the change is cheap enough that this alone is not an objection.

Postgres has no existing feature, extension or tool that reports the page size of the main shared memory segment, including on Windows; huge_pages_status reports only whether huge pages are in use. Placing the size in PGShmemHeader extends the existing accessor and adds no second mechanism, so this angle has no objection.

There is no demand objection to raise. 0001 fixes a latent bug: an exported accessor that returns zero on Windows with large pages, at small cost and with no new user surface. 0002 rests partly on resizable shared memory, which is not yet committed, but its cost is one header field that only the accessor reads, and it removes duplicated platform logic.
